items.title: Development and external validation of a nomogram for predicting in-hospital mortality in status epilepticus patients in the intensive care unit: A MIMIC-IV and eICU-CRD study.
items.abstract: To develop and externally validate a nomogram for predicting in-hospital mortality in ICU patients with SE, using readily available clinical data collected within the first 24 h of ICU admission. We identified adult SE patients from MIMIC-IV (training cohort, 2008-2019) using ICD-9/ICD-10 codes. Twenty-seven candidate predictors were screened by LASSO logistic regression with 10-fold cross-validation. The final model was constructed with multivariable logistic regression and presented as a nomogram. Internal validation used 1000 bootstrap resamples with optimism correction. External validation was performed in an independent SE cohort from the eICU-CRD database (2014-2015). The training cohort comprised 299 patients (69 deaths, 23.1% mortality). LASSO selected nine predictors: age, first ICU care unit, Glasgow Coma Scale, temperature, SpO 2 , white blood cell count, glucose, bicarbonate, and the Elixhauser comorbidity index. The optimism-corrected AUC was .807 (95% CI, .754-.860) with a Brier score of .124. External validation in 597 eICU patients yielded an AUC of .750 (95% CI, .685-.815). In sensitivity analyses, a reduced model without the comorbidity score achieved an optimism-corrected AUC of .786 and an external AUC of .730, and a model without the ICU care-unit type achieved .817 and .764, respectively. This nine-variable nomogram provides a validated, bedside-applicable tool for mortality risk stratification in ICU SE patients, enabling manual risk calculation without electronic computation.

items.title: Look Beyond the Trabeculae: CMR-Substrate Predicts Risk.
Identifying the High-Risk Arrhythmic Mitral Valve Prolapse Phenotype by Imaging.
items.abstract: Within arrhythmogenic mitral valve prolapse (AMVP), a distinct subset of mitral valve prolapse (MVP), there is a small group that carries a higher risk of malignant ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death called malignant MVP. The malignant MVP phenotype is over-represented in young women with unexplained sudden cardiac death on autopsy. AMVP is defined by myxomatous, often bileaflet MVP with mitral annular disjunction, abnormal valvular-myocardial mechanics, complex ventricular ectopy, and nonsustained ventricular tachycardia. Excessive mechanical force from systolic annular expansion, papillary muscle traction, and basal inferolateral "curling" promotes focal replacement and diffuse interstitial fibrosis, creating an arrhythmogenic substrate. Premature ventricular contractions act as triggers, whereas autonomic modulation influences the timing of ventricular arrhythmia initiation and progression to ventricular fibrillation or sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Baseline evaluation with an electrocardiogram and transthoracic echocardiography is necessary to identify AMVP, exclude severe mitral regurgitation, and identify high-risk markers. If no premature ventricular contractions are found on a resting electrocardiogram, exercise stress testing and extended rhythm monitoring can help bring out ventricular premature contractions, which are triggers of ventricular arrhythmias. Cardiac magnetic resonance provides incremental prognostic value with late gadolinium enhancement reflecting replacement fibrosis and T1 mapping identifying diffuse fibrosis, even in those with no late gadolinium enhancement. Machine-learning analysis may further refine risk stratification by integrating high-risk features such as mitral annular disjunction, fibrosis extent, and location that outperform symptom-based assessment. As transcatheter and surgical mitral interventions expand, accurate phenotyping of AMVP is increasingly important, as hemodynamic correction of mitral regurgitation alone does not eliminate the underlying arrhythmogenic substrate. Comprehensive multimodality imaging and integrated rhythm assessment are therefore central to individualized risk stratification and management in this vulnerable population.

items.title: From the Paced QRS to Assessing the Mechanical Substrate for Achieving Cardiac Resynchronization: A Leap of Faith or the Ground Truth?
Cardiac Manifestations of EGPA: An Overlap Phenotype of Inflammatory Myocardial Injury and Takotsubo-Like Syndrome.
items.abstract: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) often presents with eosinophilic myocarditis, but the spectrum of cardiac findings is scarcely reported. We describe a case of EGPA with an unusual presentation of acute left ventricular (LV) dysfunction associated with lymphocyte-predominant myocardial inflammation and Takotsubo-like syndrome with LV thrombus. A 42-year-old woman with history of asthma presented with chronic cough, dyspnea, and rash. Findings of peripheral eosinophilia, cutaneous vasculitis, mononeuritis multiplex, and myocardial inflammation confirmed antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies-negative EGPA. Her course was complicated by transient severe LV systolic dysfunction with Takotsubo-like regional wall-motion abnormalities, lymphocyte-predominant myocardial inflammation on biopsy, and LV thrombus. Management included pulse-dosed steroids, rituximab, and mepolizumab. Although EGPA frequently causes cardiac manifestations, typically eosinophilic myocarditis, an overlap phenotype of inflammatory myocardial injury, Takotsubo-like cardiomyopathy, and LV thrombus is exceedingly rare. Cardiac involvement remains the leading cause of mortality in EGPA. This case highlights the heterogeneity of its cardiac phenotypes, illustrating the importance of early cardiology evaluation and diagnostics.

items.title: CRISPR-Cas9 screen identifies eIF4G2 as a regulator of CD8+ T cell dysfunction.
items.abstract: CD8+ T cells directly target and kill cancer cells and are required for effective antitumor immunity. However, CD8+ T cells may become dysfunctional when exposed to chronic antigen stimulation during cancer. Dysfunction is characterized by reduced proliferation, increased expression of inhibitory receptors, and impaired effector function, yet the genetic mechanisms controlling dysfunction remain poorly understood. Therefore, we developed a murine ex vivo chronic stimulation model that recapitulates features of CD8+ T cell dysfunction observed within the tumor microenvironment. By coupling this system with genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 loss-of-function screening, we discovered that the progression of murine CD8+ T cells to a dysfunctional state required eIF4G2, a noncanonical mRNA translation factor. Deletion of eIF4G2 restored CD8+ T cell survival and proliferation during chronic stimulation conditions in vitro. Transcriptomic, proteomic, and flow cytometric analyses revealed that eIF4G2 deletion shifts CD8+ T cell phenotype from a dysfunctional state to a proliferative state. eIF4G2 depletion reduced oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and accumulation of misfolded protein aggresomes during chronic in vitro stimulation. Finally, eIF4G2-depleted cells mediated enhanced tumor control in a murine model of melanoma. These data suggest that targeting eIF4G2 may promote CD8+ T cell resilience and improve therapeutic antitumor immunity.

items.title: Claudin 18.2: From a Tight Junction Protein to a Breakthrough Target in Solid Tumor Immunotherapy.
items.abstract: Claudin 18.2 (CLDN18.2), a tight junction protein largely confined to normal gastric mucosa, is overexpressed and mislocalized on the surface of gastric, gastroesophageal, pancreatic, and other gastrointestinal cancers. This pattern has made CLDN18.2 a leading target in solid tumor immunotherapy. This review traces its path from a structural junctional component to a clinically relevant antigen and assesses the therapeutic platforms built around it. We discuss monoclonal antibodies, especially zolbetuximab, whose phase III SPOTLIGHT and GLOW trials improved survival in CLDN18.2-positive, HER2-negative gastric and gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma and led to regulatory approval. We then evaluate antibody-drug conjugates, bispecific T-cell engagers, and CAR T-cell therapies, comparing their mechanisms, efficacy, toxicity, and resistance. We also examine the rationale for combining CLDN18.2-directed agents with immune checkpoint inhibitors, although clinical evidence for synergy remains indirect. Major challenges include antigen loss and heterogeneity, autophagy-mediated ADC resistance, on-target gastrointestinal toxicity, cytokine release syndrome, and unstandardized expression thresholds. Because optimal cutoffs differ by modality, patient selection should follow the intended therapeutic class rather than a universal biomarker score. Overall, CLDN18.2-directed therapy is a maturing precision oncology strategy; its impact will depend on randomized data, better biomarkers, and rational combinations.

items.title: Recent Immunoglobulin G1 Engineering Strategies to Modulate Immune Effector Functions for Therapeutics.
items.abstract: IgG is the most common scaffold used for antibody-based therapeutics. Utilization of the ever-expanding knowledge base of the IgG scaffold provides a wealth of design options for therapeutic development. These therapeutics apply varied engineering strategies in various combinations utilizing three key IgG features: the crystallizable fragment (Fc), antigen-binding fragment (Fab), and the conserved N-glycans. Designs may be as simple as amino acid variants to modulate effector function or as complex as large designs incorporating additional Fab, Fc, and non-IgG domain fusions to modulate effector molecule recognition, valency, and antigen specificity. The engineering strategies and basic knowledge supporting these developments have been the subject of rapid expansion. Here we review multiple approaches and advances with a focus on the last five years.

items.title: A guide to studying tumour-T-cell interactions using in vitro coculture assays.
items.abstract: T cells are central mediators of antitumour immunity and are the cellular basis of many successful cancer immunotherapies, including immune checkpoint blockade, T-cell receptor (TCR)-engineered therapies and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells. However, clinical responses remain variable, and many tumours evade or resist T-cell-mediated control. Understanding how T cells recognise tumour cells, deliver cytotoxic signals, produce inflammatory cytokines and shape tumour cell fate is therefore essential for improving modern immunotherapies. In vitro tumour T-cell coculture systems provide a powerful experimental framework for dissecting these processes under controlled conditions. They allow investigators to manipulate antigen specificity, HLA/MHC restriction, tumour genotype, T-cell activation state, cytokine exposure and drug-mediated perturbation in ways that are difficult to achieve in vivo. However, these systems require careful design, because assay outcomes are strongly influenced by tumour model, antigen expression, effector-to-target ratio, assay duration and readout. This guide provides a practical framework for studying tumour T-cell interactions in vitro, with a focus on CD8+ T-cell-mediated tumour recognition and killing. It discusses commonly used mouse and human antigen-specific models, how antigen expression and presentation can be experimentally controlled, T-cell activation and coculture conditions, cytotoxicity assays, immune synapse imaging, competition assays, cytokine-mediated bystander killing, transcriptional profiling, CRISPR perturbation strategies, therapeutic testing and patient-derived models. The aim is to help researchers choose the most appropriate model, experimental setup and readout for the biological question being asked and to avoid common interpretive pitfalls when studying tumour immune sensitivity, resistance and therapeutic response.

items.title: Harnessing the Bacterial Membrane-Derived Oral Vaccine to Potentiate Antitumor Immunity and Metabolic Control of T Cells.
items.abstract: The fluctuating gastrointestinal milieu and its restrictive epithelial barrier represent critical challenges for the design of oral cancer vaccines. Nevertheless, leveraging the gut microbiome as an interventional strategy has recently gained traction, especially in patients on immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy. Here, microbial-derived double-layered membrane vesicles are developed as adjuvants and cell-free carriers, fused with cell-penetrating peptide-modified antigens, and encapsulated in an alginate/chitosan-microsystem to engineer oral vaccines. This design strategically harnesses the crosstalk between the gut microbiome and gut-associated lymphoid tissues, driving dendritic cell maturation, plasma cell activation, and production of immune-stimulatory cytokines within the mesenteric lymph nodes and lamina propria. In mouse prophylactic and therapeutic tumor models, the select Bifidobacterium bifidum-derived oral vaccine combined with anti-PD1 treatment enhances cytotoxic antitumor responses, along with Th1-, Th17-immunity, leading to potent tumor suppression, prolonged survival, and long-term protection against tumor rechallenge. Mechanistically, the vaccine promotes interferon-γ-producing T cells and antitumor efficacy with ICI therapy via the improved microbiota diversity and signaling metabolites, with an indole-3-acetic-acid (3IAA) enriched diet profoundly shaping T-cell recruitment and differentiation. Our findings uncover a tryptophan metabolite-driven immune axis that amplifies the specific antitumor immune response, redefining oral vaccines as a powerful tool for cancer immunotherapy.

items.title: Tobevibart plus elebsiran in hepatitis D: crossing a therapeutic threshold.
Preoperative portal vein thrombosis did not compromise long-term survival after liver transplantation with proper portal inflow reconstruction.
items.abstract: Portal vein thrombosis (PVT) increases operative complexity and complication risks in liver transplantation (LT), but whether it compromises long-term survival with proper portal inflow reconstruction remains debated. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of preoperative PVT on perioperative and long-term outcomes after LT and to assess outcomes following individualized portal inflow reconstruction in patients with complex PVT. Adult orthotopic LT recipients between 2016 and 2024 were retrospectively recruited and stratified into PVT (n=144) and non-PVT (n=373) groups. Baseline, operative, and survival data were compared. PVT patients had higher rates of Child-Pugh B/C (86.2% vs. 74.8%), hepatic encephalopathy (30.6% vs. 20.6%), upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB; 57.6% vs. 35.9%), and prior splenectomy (16.7% vs. 2.4%; all P vs. 75.1%), longer operative time (453 vs. 405 min), greater blood loss (1,200 vs. 800 mL), and more red blood cell transfusions (800 vs. 600 mL; all P vs. 3.5%) and 1-year renal dysfunction (52.5% vs. 39.4%) were more frequent in the PVT group (P<0.05). However, preoperative PVT was not an independent predictor of long-term survival in Kaplan-Meier or Cox regression. Preoperative PVT did not compromise long-term survival after LT but increased operative complexity, PV-related complications, and renal dysfunction. When appropriately designed, a non-anatomical portal reconstruction strategy could achieve favorable outcomes in complex PVT cases.

items.title: Pancreatic solid papillary neoplasm with high-grade malignant transformation and multiple hepatic metastases in an elderly male: a case report.
items.abstract: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasms (SPNs) are rare pancreatic tumors that predominantly affect young women and generally exhibit low malignant potential. High-grade malignant transformation with distant metastasis is uncommon, particularly in elderly males. A 66-year-old male with hepatitis B virus-related cirrhosis presented with obstructive jaundice, abdominal pain, and significant weight loss. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed a large pancreatic head mass with multiple hepatic lesions. Histopathological examination demonstrated mixed solid and pseudopapillary architecture with marked nuclear atypia, high mitotic activity, and extensive necrosis. Immunohistochemical analysis showed nuclear β-catenin positivity and expression of CD56 and CD99, with negative neuroendocrine markers, and a proliferative Ki-67 labeling index of approximately 60% in the hot spot together, these findings confirmed SPN with high-grade malignant transformation and hepatic metastases. This case represents an aggressive and atypical presentation of an SPN. Advanced disease, extensive metastases, and underlying liver cirrhosis significantly limited therapeutic options; only palliative management was feasible. High-grade metastatic SPNs may exhibit aggressive clinical behavior and a poor prognosis. Elderly male sex may represent a potential adverse prognostic factor for aggressive SPN variants. Early recognition and accurate diagnosis are essential, particularly in atypical populations with significant comorbidities.

items.title: Community-based interventions to improve hepatitis C linkage to care among people with substance use disorders in Southwest Virginia: a pragmatic sequential cohort study.
items.abstract: In 2024, the reported hepatitis C virus (HCV) case rate in Roanoke City was nearly three times the rate of the state of Virginia, reflecting the disproportionate impact of the opioid epidemic in the region. Despite highly effective direct-acting antiviral therapies, substantial barriers to linkage to care (LTC) persist among individuals with substance use disorders (SUDs). While prior studies suggest that patient navigation and financial support may improve LTC, evidence from rural and underserved settings remains limited. This study aims to evaluate community-based interventions designed to improve HCV LTC among individuals with SUD in Southwest Virginia. We conducted a pragmatic, non-randomized, sequential cohort pilot study to evaluate the impact of iteratively refined community-based interventions on LTC. A total of 60 adults with detectable HCV RNA and SUD were enrolled sequentially into four cohorts (control and three intervention groups). All participants received peer support; intervention components were modified across cohorts to address observed barriers to care. The primary outcome was attendance at an outpatient HCV visit within 180 days of enrolment. LTC was 3/15 (20%) in both the control group and Intervention 1, increasing to 6/15 (40%) in Intervention 2 and 11/15 (73%) in Intervention 3. Exploratory analyses demonstrated significantly higher attendance in Intervention 3 than in the control group (73% vs. 20%, P  = .009). Telehealth utilization and provision of prepaid phones were incorporated in the final cohort, which demonstrated the highest LTC rate. Multicomponent community-based interventions were associated with improved LTC among individuals with SUD. Although the non-randomized sequential design limits causal attribution, the progressive improvement across cohorts provides preliminary support for a potential benefit. Interventions incorporating community navigation, telehealth access, and communication support may help address barriers to HCV treatment engagement in underserved communities.

items.title: Viral persistence and immune dysfunction in chronic hepatitis B: Mechanisms of post-treatment antigen asynchrony.
items.abstract: Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) remains a major global health burden. Following antiviral therapy, the dynamics of hepatitis B virus (HBV) DNA and hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) may become discordant, a phenomenon referred to as post-treatment asynchrony. This review summarizes the three principal forms of post-treatment asynchrony and examines their underlying mechanisms. We integrate the limitations of current antiviral targets, host immune dysfunction, virological characteristics, and host genetic factors into a unified framework to explain the discordant dynamics between HBsAg and HBV DNA. A better understanding of post-treatment asynchrony may help refine the interpretation of serological markers and inform patient stratification and individualized therapeutic strategies. Overall, this review provides an integrated perspective on the mechanisms and clinical significance of post-treatment asynchrony in CHB.

items.title: Pediatric Liver Transplantation in the Treatment of Solid Liver Tumors: A Narrative Review.
items.abstract: Pediatric primary liver malignancies comprise a heterogeneous group of tumors requiring individualized multidisciplinary management. Hepatoblastoma and hepatocellular carcinoma remain the most common malignant liver tumors in children, whereas rare hepatic neoplasms account for a small but clinically significant proportion of cases. Over the past two decades, advances in tumor biology, standardized radiologic staging, multidisciplinary treatment planning, and liver transplantation have substantially improved outcomes, particularly for children with unresectable hepatoblastoma. Contemporary management has shifted from an anatomy-based approach to individualized treatment strategies that integrate molecular characterization, PRETEXT staging, response to neoadjuvant therapy, and careful assessment of surgical resectability. Liver transplantation is now recognized as a definitive oncologic treatment for carefully selected children with unresectable hepatoblastoma, selected cases of hepatocellular carcinoma, and, in exceptional circumstances, other rare hepatic malignancies. In parallel, improvements in post-transplant oncologic surveillance and immunosuppressive management have expanded opportunities for long-term disease control while emphasizing the need to balance graft preservation with recurrence risk. Emerging technologies, including molecular biomarkers, liquid biopsy, artificial intelligence, and advanced surgical planning, together with international collaborative initiatives, are expected to further refine patient selection and post-transplant management. This review summarizes current evidence on the role of liver transplantation in pediatric liver malignancies and discusses contemporary advances reshaping pediatric transplant oncology.

items.title: Prognostic factors in thyroid cancer with lung-only metastasis: SEER-based retrospective study.
items.abstract: Lung-only metastasis in thyroid cancer is uncommon, and its prognostic determinants remain poorly defined. This study aimed to investigate the clinicopathological features and prognostic factors associated with survival in patients with primary thyroid cancer with lung-only metastases (PTCSLMs). Patients diagnosed with PTCSLMs from 2010 to 2015 were screened from the National Cancer Institute's Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database. Inclusion criteria comprised histologically confirmed thyroid cancer, first primary malignancy, and lung‑only metastasis at initial diagnosis, while patients with bone/liver/brain metastases, unknown race, unknown T stage/T 0 , or missing survival data were excluded. Variables analyzed included demographics (age, sex, marital status, race), clinicopathological features (histological subtype, T stage, N stage, grade stage), and treatment modalities {surgery, radiotherapy [external beam radiation therapy (EBRT)/radioactive iodine (RAI)/others], and chemotherapy}. Overall survival (OS) was defined as time from diagnosis to death from any cause, and cancer-specific survival (CSS) as time to thyroid cancer‑specific death. Univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards model were used to identify prognostic factors of PTCSLMs. The Kaplan-Meier method was used to generate survival curves, and the difference was compared using the log-rank test. A total of 592 patients diagnosed with PTCSLMs from 2010 to 2015 were extracted from the SEER database based on the specified criteria for inclusion and exclusion. Univariate analysis demonstrated statistically significant associations between OS and age at diagnosis, marital status, histologic subtype, T stage, N stage, grade stage, surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy (P 0.001). The results of multivariate survival analyses showed that age at diagnosis [43-80 vs. 6-42 years, hazard ratio (HR) =5.044, 95% confidence interval (CI): 2.290-11.111, P 0.001; 81-99 vs. 6-42 years, HR =7.769, 95% CI: 3.296-18.312, P 0.001], histologic subtype [others vs. papillary adenocarcinoma (PA), HR =1.786, 95% CI: 1.323-2.411, P 0.001], T stage (T 2 vs. T X , HR =0.480, 95% CI: 0.247-0.935, P = 0.03), grade stage (poorly differentiated vs. well differentiated, HR =1.976, 95% CI: 1.123-3.476, P = 0.02; undifferentiated vs. well differentiated, HR =2.531, 95% CI: 1.417-4.521, P = 0.002), surgery (total thyroidectomy vs. refuse/none, HR =0.387, 95% CI: 0.278-0.538, P 0.001; others vs. refuse/none, HR =0.663, 95% CI: 0.455-0.967, P = 0.03), radiotherapy (EBRT vs. refuse/none/unknown, HR =0.734, 95% CI: 0.564-0.955, P = 0.02; RAI vs. refuse/none/unknown, HR =0.481, 95% CI: 0.336-0.688, P 0.001; others vs. refuse/none/unknown, HR =0.498, 95% CI: 0.254-0.978, P = 0.043) and chemotherapy (yes vs. no/unknown, HR =0.741, 95%CI: 0.560-0.982, P = 0.04) were independent prognostic factors of PTCSLMs. Our study suggested that the higher age at diagnosis and higher pathological grade were correlated with worse prognosis. In contrast, surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy showed a favorable prognostic association. Age at diagnosis, histological type, T stage, grade stage, surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy are associated with prognosis and they are independent prognostic factors for PTCSLMs.

items.title: Comparison between operative management versus non-operative management in patients with solid organ blunt abdominal injury in the National Trauma Registry of Iran.
items.abstract: Trauma is one of the leading causes of death worldwide. Severe abdominal injuries cause one-fifth of injury mortality. Non-operative management (NOM) or operative management (OM) is a primary challenge in abdominal injuries. In this study, we aimed to compare NOM and OM outcomes in patients with solid organ blunt abdominal injuries in the National Trauma Registry of Iran (NTRI). This cross-sectional study was conducted with data from the NTRI from 24 July 2016 to 21 May 2023. All patients with a solid organ abdominal injury by road traffic crash, falls, hit or bodily force, and assault with blunt objects were admitted to trauma registry member hospitals across the country, according to the NTRI criteria included in this study. Among 358 patients, liver, spleen, and kidney single-organ injuries were managed non-operative more than operative. Among multi-organ abdomen injuries, kidney injuries alongside spleen or liver injuries are managed non-operative more than operative. In the multiple regression model on the matched cohort (102 NOM with 102 OM), moderate or severe Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) had 16.79 times more chance of Intensive Care Unit (ICU) admission than mild GCS [OR: 16.79, 95% CI (2.06, 137.22), P = 0.008]. Also, hypovolemia increased the chance of death 12.9 times [OR: 12.90, 95% CI (2.20, 75.53), P = 0.005]. In addition, for every 1-year increase in age, the odds of the death occurring increased 1.07 [OR: 1.07, 95% CI (1.02, 1.12), P = 0.005]. We observed the non-inferiority of NOM than OM due to the outcomes. Although the liver, spleen, and kidney are mainly managed by non-operatives.

items.title: Distinguishing Second Primary Müllerian Cancer from Breast Cancer Recurrence: Immunohistochemical Pitfalls and a Proposed Diagnostic Algorithm: A Case Report and Literature Review.
items.abstract: Distinguishing a second primary Müllerian high‑grade serous carcinoma (HGSC) from metastatic breast cancer in survivors is a diagnostic challenge, especially when peritoneal carcinomatosis occurs without an adnexal mass. We report a 48‑year‑old woman with prior luminal B breast cancer who presented with liver and abdominal wall nodules. Initially misdiagnosed as breast cancer recurrence based on limited immunohistochemistry (IHC), she received 12 months of ineffective therapy. Repeat biopsy with an extended panel (PAX8+, WT1+, p53 mutant‑type, GATA3 weak/partial, GCDFP‑15-) established primary HGSC. A literature review of comparative IHC studies identifies key pitfalls: TRPS1 is positive in 40-47% of HGSCs in large cohorts, with some series reporting up to 70%; PAX8 with the MRQ50 clone is falsely positive in 40% of triple‑negative breast cancers (TNBC); and GATA3 shows weak/focal positivity in 6-13% of HGSCs. A proposed six‑marker panel (PAX8, WT1, GATA3, p53, GCDFP‑15, TRPS1) is recommended to prevent misdiagnosis and expedite appropriate platinum‑based therapy and cytoreductive surgery.
